title: Problem 1 (Fitzsimons; Angel and Holroyd)
context_text: Fitzsimons raised this question on Stack Exchange in 2011 and Angel and Holroyd independently asked it in 2018; both had given constructions of transposition shuffles achieving length $\binom{n}{2}$ and asked whether this is optimal. The paper resolves the question negatively.
paper_contribution: Answers Problem 1 negatively: constructs a transposition shuffle of length $(1-\varepsilon)\binom{n}{2}$ for some $\varepsilon>0$ and all $n\geq 6$, and more precisely of length $\frac{2}{3}\binom{n}{2}+O(n\log n)$.

title: Problem 3
context_text: A lazy transposition $(a,b,p)$ is the random permutation equal to the transposition $(a,b)$ with probability $p$ and to the identity otherwise. Think of $t$ distinguishable counters placed initially in positions $1,\dots,t$ among $n$ positions; a lazy transposition $(a,b,p)$ swaps the contents of positions $a$ and $b$ (possibly a counter and an empty position) with probability $p$. A sequence of independent lazy transpositions is a $(t,n)$-shuffle if the final placement of the counters is uniformly distributed over all $t!\binom{n}{t}$ possibilities, and $U_t(n)$ is the minimum length of a $(t,n)$-shuffle; $U(n)=U_n(n)$ is the minimum length of a sequence whose composition is a uniformly random permutation of $S_n$. Simple sweeping and divide-and-conquer constructions give $U_t(n)\le tn-\binom{t+1}{2}$. For $t=n$ the question is the problem of Fitzsimons and of Angel and Holroyd whether $U(n)=\binom n2$, which the authors answer negatively: $U(n)\le(1-\varepsilon)\binom n2$ for $n\ge6$ and $U(n)\le\frac23\binom n2+O(n\log n)$. Note that the paper also answers this question negatively for every $3\le t\le n$ with $n\ge6$: $U_t(n)\le(1-\varepsilon)(tn-\binom{t+1}{2})$ for an absolute $\varepsilon>0$. For $t=2$, they found no $(2,n)$-shuffle with fewer than $2n-3=2n-\binom32$ lazy transpositions and conjecture that $U_2(n)=2n-3$ for $n\ge2$.
